sections.title: Name and identification
sections.text: The poplar fieldcap is listed as Cyclocybe cylindracea by the German and Swiss mushroom lists and many European guides; the name Cyclocybe aegerita is also in use, including in this app's stable identifier. Expanded caps are about 4–10 cm across, hemispherical when young, then broadly convex or nearly flat. They are pale buff with a richer brown central zone; dry weather can make the surface crack. Crowded gills attach to the stem or run slightly down it, changing from cream to grey-brown and then mid brown. The firm creamy-white stem browns with age and has a persistent drooping membranous ring. The spore print is tobacco brown. Odour is generally pleasant, but is not a reliable identification test.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This wood-decaying fungus fruits in tufts on stumps and standing dead or declining broadleaf trees, especially poplars and willows; it can also occur on hardwood chips. In Britain and Ireland it is mainly seen from July to October, while fruiting may continue later in milder southern European regions. The species is also cultivated, but a wild cluster requires independent identification.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: Other brown-capped, ringed mushrooms can grow on wood. Kuehneromyces mutabilis is generally smaller, more hygrophanous and scaly below the ring; its brown spore print does not by itself exclude confusion. Deadly Galerina marginata is another wood-growing brown mushroom with a fragile ring and brown spores, and must be ruled out before any food use. Cap cracks, tree host, smell and ring alone are insufficient to confirm the species; an expert should examine all characters of each collected specimen.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: The German Mycological Society and Swiss VAPKO include the poplar fieldcap under C. cylindracea on their recommended edible lists. First Nature also describes it as edible. That classification does not make a photograph a safe basis for eating wild specimens. Do not consume an uncertain identification or a mixed tuft. If ingestion is followed by illness, or a dangerous lookalike cannot be excluded, contact a poison centre or medical service promptly and retain specimens or the meal remains.

traits: Buff 4–10 cm cap with darker brown centre, often cracked in dry weather
Crowded attached to slightly descending gills, cream then grey-brown
Firm pale stem browning with age and a persistent drooping membranous ring
Tobacco-brown spore print; pleasant smell is not a decisive test
Tufts on poplar, willow or other dead broadleaf wood, summer to autumn
safetyNote: Listed as edible under the name Cyclocybe cylindracea by specialist bodies, but wild brown wood-growing mushrooms include dangerous lookalikes such as Galerina marginata. Do not eat a specimen identified only from this image or from one trait; seek expert confirmation. After uncertain ingestion or illness, seek prompt poison-centre or medical advice.
